pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 9–11, Reading Weather Maps (PROCEDURAL) — interpret weather-map symbols (temperature, precipitation, wind), read data tables and graphs to spot trends over weeks/months/seasons, and use the data to make simple predictions.
• Standards — UK (DfE): KS2 working scientifically — record, present and interpret data; use graphs and tables to answer questions and identify patterns.
• Standards — US (NGSS): builds directly on 3-ESS2-1 ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 3-ESS2-1]'); extends from recording to INTERPRETING and predicting. State/regional tier DEFERRED.
• Operational details: teach a symbol key first, then move from single-map reading to spotting TRENDS across a data series, then to using the trend to predict; stress that a prediction is a probability read from a pattern, not a certainty; use real Met Office/NOAA-style maps and the class's own recorded data.
• Checkpoint (Tier A|B|C): Tier A — interpret common map symbols; Tier B — read a table/graph and identify a pattern; Tier C — use the data to make and justify a prediction.
bestPractices: Teach the symbol key explicitly before interpretation — temperature, precipitation, wind arrows/barbs, fronts
Progress from reading a single map to spotting TRENDS across a time series of data
Make prediction the payoff — use the identified pattern to forecast, then check against what happened
Frame predictions as probabilities read from patterns, not guarantees
Use authentic maps and the pupils' own weather-diary data so interpretation has real referents
keyRepresentations: An annotated weather map with a tappable symbol key
A time-series graph/table of temperature or rainfall showing a trend
Front/pressure symbols linked to the weather they bring
commonMisconceptions: A weather map shows the weather everywhere all the time — it is a snapshot/forecast for a moment or period
A single data point shows a trend — trends need a series of readings
Predictions from data are certainties — they are probabilities read from patterns
All symbols are self-evident — many (fronts, wind barbs, pressure) must be decoded from a key
Higher numbers always mean 'worse' weather — units and what is measured matter

learn.summary: Learners aged 9–11 practise the procedural skill of reading weather maps: decoding map symbols (temperature, precipitation, wind), extracting specific values from data tables and graphs, spotting trends across a time series, and using a pattern to make a justified, probabilistic prediction. Teach the symbol key explicitly first, then move from single-map reading to trend-spotting across a series, then to predict-then-check with authentic maps and the class's own weather-diary data.

activities.title: Crack the code: decode a real weather map
feedback: If a wind direction seems reversed, return to this map’s key. Meteorological wind is named by where it comes from; a motion arrow may point where it goes, while a conventional wind-barb staff extends toward the direction it comes from.
If a learner assumes a symbol is self-evident, point back to the key and ask them to decode fronts, wind barbs or pressure explicitly.
Read wind speed only from the encodings this map specifies, such as barb feathers, a numeric label, arrow length or colour. Do not infer a speed when the key gives no speed encoding.
If a learner says the map shows the weather everywhere all the time, clarify it is a snapshot or forecast for a particular moment or period.
activities.rationale: Explicit symbol-key decoding is the first step of the procedure; several symbols cannot be inferred without a key, and confusing the direction a wind symbol points with the direction the wind comes from is a common reversal error. A tap-to-reveal key on a map makes the decoding mechanism concrete.
sourceClaims: Weather-map symbols (fronts, wind barbs, pressure) must be decoded from a key, and data-based forecasts are probabilistic patterns rather than certainties.
learnerActions: Study a labelled weather map showing temperature figures, weather icons (e.g. sun, cloud, rain), wind symbols (arrows or barbs), and front/pressure symbols.

Use the actual map’s key to decode temperature, precipitation, fronts, pressure and wind. State wind direction and speed only as encoded by that key, including any arrow length, colour, label or barb markings.

Name wind by the direction it comes from. Check the map’s key to decide whether a wind arrow points toward its destination or a staff extends toward its origin, and translate that symbol into the correct from-direction.
Explain, for a named front or pressure symbol, what weather it tends to bring.
activities.intendedInsight: A weather map is a decodable instrument, not decoration: many symbols (fronts, wind barbs, pressure) must be read from a key rather than guessed, and a map is a snapshot/forecast for a moment or period, not the weather everywhere all the time.

activities.title: Read the data and name the trend
feedback: If a learner misreads the graph axis or reads between gridlines wrongly, have them track from the point to the labelled axis and re-check the units; a value off the scale or the wrong day signals this error.
If a learner treats one day's value as the whole pattern, prompt: look across all the points before naming a pattern.
If a learner assumes a high number means bad weather, ask what is being measured and in what units.
activities.rationale: Extracting accurate values and distinguishing a single point from a genuine trend are core to the 'read a table/graph and identify a pattern' objective. A scrubber or slider across a week/season of data can make the emerging trend visible as an optional interaction.
sourceClaims: DfE KS2 working scientifically requires recording, presenting and interpreting data and using tables/graphs to identify patterns and answer questions.
learnerActions: Read a time-series table or graph of weather data (e.g. temperature or rainfall over a week, month or season).
Extract specific values when asked: the highest temperature, which day was wettest, the value on a named day.
Track a finger from each data point to the labelled axis and check the units before reporting a value.
Look across ALL the data points and name the trend (e.g. temperatures rising through the week, rainfall decreasing, pressure falling).
activities.intendedInsight: A trend requires a series of readings — a single data point is not a pattern — and correct reading depends on checking the axis scale and units, since higher numbers do not automatically mean 'worse' weather.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: forecast tomorrow from the pattern
feedback: If a learner predicts with no reference to the trend ('it'll be sunny because I like sun'), ask: what does the trend across the week suggest?
If a learner treats the prediction as a certainty, discuss why forecasts are probabilities and why a mismatch does not mean the method failed.
Prompt the learner to justify: if the trend kept going, what would the day after tomorrow look like?
activities.rationale: The predict-then-verify loop rehearses the 'use data to make a prediction' objective and directly targets the misconception that predictions are certainties. Committing before revealing the outcome makes the probabilistic framing concrete.
sourceClaims: Weather-map symbols (fronts, wind barbs, pressure) must be decoded from a key, and data-based forecasts are probabilistic patterns rather than certainties.
learnerActions: Read the trend across the data series for a named place.
Commit to a prediction for tomorrow's (or the next period's) conditions, explicitly grounding it in the observed pattern.
Reveal or record the actual outcome and compare it with the prediction.
Reflect on matches and mismatches, articulating that a forecast is a probability read from a pattern, not a guarantee.
activities.intendedInsight: A data-based prediction is a probability read from a pattern — it should be justified by the trend and may still turn out wrong; this is the payoff of interpreting the map and data.

activities.title: Symbol- and graph-reading checks (companion assessment)
feedback: For a wrong symbol answer, return to the key (and, for wind, check that map's own direction convention and whether the direction or the speed encoding was misread).
For a graph-reading error, re-track from point to axis and re-check units.
For an ungrounded prediction, ask which trend in the data supports it.
activities.rationale: Short targeted questions map onto all three evidence objectives and provide a fixed-format check of interpretation. Note this format checks recognition and single-step reading; it does not, on its own, reveal the live procedural errors a performance task exposes.
learnerActions: Answer targeted questions: 'What does this symbol mean?', 'What pattern does this graph show?', and 'Predict from this data.'
Select or state the correct value read from a specific graph or table.
Choose or state a prediction that follows from the shown trend and justify the choice.
activities.intendedInsight: Symbol meaning, pattern identification, and data-based prediction can each be checked directly, surfacing whether the learner can apply the interpretation procedure.

constraints: Teach the symbol key explicitly before any interpretation — temperature, precipitation, wind arrows/barbs, fronts, pressure.
Wind is named by its from-direction, but the orientation convention of the displayed symbol must be read from its key. Do not apply one FROM-arrow rule to every map.

Teach the wind-symbol conventions used by the selected authentic map: conventional barbs encode direction with the staff and speed with feathers/flags; other maps may encode speed with labels, arrow size or colour. Always follow the key.
Progress in order: single-map reading → trend-spotting across a time series → predicting from the trend; do not skip to prediction.
Frame predictions as probabilities read from patterns, not guarantees; a mismatch between forecast and actual is expected and instructive.
Use authentic Met Office/NOAA-style maps and the pupils' own recorded weather-diary data so interpretation has real referents.

A static labelled image with a tap-to-reveal key can teach symbol decoding but does not let learners exercise trend-spotting or the predict-then-check loop; use it as a decoding scaffold, not the whole procedure.

Recognition/selection checks (choosing a symbol meaning or value) verify reading but do not elicit the independent, observable procedure of working across a map and data to predict; pair them with a performance task where feasible.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original row rated 3D interpretation as 'adding nothing' and dialogue as unable to teach this skill; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been softened — flat maps/graphs/tables have no spatial-depth requirement so 3D offers no obvious affordance here, and discussion can still support reflection even if decoding and predicting are the core practice.
The claim that 'a static image can't exercise trend-spotting and prediction' has been reframed as a scaffold limit rather than a universal law.

Two source claims (DfE KS2; Met Office/NOAA resource) are marked verified:false in the row; treat their support as unconfirmed. The NGSS claim (verified:true) concerns representing data to describe seasonal weather and frames the basis this interpret-and-predict topic extends, but its direct support for the specific 'read-and-identify-trend' step is only partial, so it was not attached to that activity's sourceClaims; the DfE claim most directly supports that step.

The source mixed generic wind arrows with conventional wind barbs. Their orientation and speed encodings are not interchangeable, so activities now defer to the selected map’s actual key; wind itself is named by the direction it comes from.

probeDeeper: Show me how you found the wettest day — how did you know it was that one?
Which way is the wind blowing on this map, and how does the symbol tell you?
If the trend kept going, what would the day after tomorrow look like?
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the symbols correctly (temperature figures, rain/sun icons, wind arrows for direction and often strength), extracts specific values from the table/graph, identifies a trend (e.g. temperatures rising through the week, a front approaching) and uses the pattern to make a reasonable prediction for the named place.

errorPatterns.pattern: Reads the wind arrow as pointing where the wind is going, not where it comes from
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convention: the arrow flies FROM the direction the wind comes; name that direction.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misreads the graph axis or reads between gridlines wrongly
errorPatterns.nextMove: Track finger from the point to the labelled axis; check the units.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: reports a value off the scale or picks the wrong day

errorPatterns.pattern: Predicts tomorrow with no reference to the trend ('it'll be sunny because I like sun')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask: 'what does the trend across the week suggest?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: prediction not grounded in the data pattern

errorPatterns.pattern: Treats one day's data point as the whole pattern
errorPatterns.nextMove: Look across all the points before naming a pattern.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: generalises a single value to a trend

responseLevels.gap: Misreads symbols or the graph; cannot extract a correct value or make a data-based prediction.
responseLevels.full: Reads all symbols and data accurately, identifies the trend, and uses it to make a reasonable prediction for the named place — reliably on a new map.
responseLevels.partial: Reads symbols and values correctly but can't identify the trend, or makes a prediction unconnected to the pattern.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a real weather map (symbols for sun, rain, wind arrows and temperatures) and a table or graph of a week's weather data. Ask them to tell you tomorrow's likely conditions for a named place, read off specific values (the highest temperature, which day was wettest) and say what pattern the data shows — then watch how they read the symbols and use the data. Don't ask them to define the symbols; watch them use them.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child work exposes procedural errors — reading a wind arrow backwards, misreading the graph axis, picking the wrong day, or predicting with no reference to the pattern — that a verbal 'what does this symbol mean?' would hide.
